title: Perform animal production and health care practices of cows and bulls

lessons.title: Daily herd observation and breeding tasks
lessons.html:
Practical herd work

In this module you will perform the hands-on production and health tasks for adult cows and bulls. Your assessor will check that you do each task correctly and safely.

Herd observation round

Walk the herd at set times each day, quietly, and look at each group:

  • Cows lying and chewing the cud, or standing restlessly?
  • Any cow alone, dull, off feed, limping or bloated?
  • Any cow showing heat signs?
  • Any close-up cow starting to calve?
  • Water troughs full and clean; fences and gates secure?

Record what you see with cow numbers and times.

Heat detection

  1. Observe at least two or three times a day for 20 to 30 minutes, outside milking and feeding times.
  2. Look for standing heat (stands to be mounted), mounting others, clear mucus, swollen vulva, restlessness.
  3. Check tail paint or heat patches: rubbed-off paint suggests the cow has been mounted.
  4. Check activity monitor alerts if the farm uses collars.
  5. Record cow number, date, time and signs; inform the AI technician according to the farm schedule.

Preparing for AI and pregnancy checks

  • Draft the cows to be served or checked into a holding pen after milking.
  • Move them calmly into the crush or feed barrier.
  • Have records ready: last calving date, previous services.
  • Record service details or pregnancy results immediately.

Drying off

On the planned date, stop milking the cow, apply dry cow treatment or teat sealant as the vet prescribes, using strict hygiene: clean and disinfect each teat end with a separate swab, insert the tube carefully, then post-dip. Mark and record the cow and move her to the dry group.

lessons.title: Health care tasks on adult cows
lessons.html:
Performing routine health care

Taking a temperature

Stand to the side of the cow, lift the tail gently, insert a clean, lubricated digital thermometer into the rectum and hold it against the wall until it beeps. Compare with the normal range on the farm chart. Clean and disinfect the thermometer afterwards.

Giving injections

  1. Confirm the cow, medicine, dose and route with the treatment instruction from the vet or supervisor.
  2. Check the label and expiry date; shake if required.
  3. Restrain the cow in a crush or head clamp.
  4. Use a clean, sharp needle of the correct size.
  5. Inject into the site specified: subcutaneous under loose neck skin, or intramuscular into the neck muscle. Avoid the rump to protect meat quality.
  6. Mark the cow, update the treatment board and record date, medicine, dose, route, batch, operator and withdrawal end dates.
  7. Put needles in the sharps container.

Treating mastitis

Follow the vet's protocol. Milk out the infected quarter, clean and disinfect the teat end, insert the intramammary tube with clean technique, post-dip, mark the cow and divert her milk.

Hoof care

  • Score locomotion regularly: watch cows walking on a flat surface.
  • Present lame cows for trimming by a trained hoof trimmer.
  • Prepare and refresh footbaths as the vet advises, wearing gloves and eye protection with chemicals.

Parasite control

Apply tick and fly treatments and dewormers according to the vet's plan and the product label. Wear the protective equipment on the label, never eat or smoke while handling, and wash afterwards. Check milk withdrawal times on the label before using any product on lactating cows.

Emergencies

Report bloat, milk fever, difficult calvings and down cows immediately. Keep the cow calm, provide shade and water, and wait for the vet or trained supervisor.

lessons.title: Handling bulls and moving cattle safely
lessons.html:
Bull management tasks

  • Bulls are tested for breeding soundness and disease by the vet before the breeding season.
  • Check bulls daily for lameness, injuries, condition and libido during the season.
  • Record which bull runs with which group and when.
  • Feed and water bulls adequately; keep them in good but not fat condition.

Bull safety rules

  1. Never enter a bull pen or camp alone. Tell someone where you are.
  2. Always know your escape route: a gap, a ladder or a solid fence you can get over.
  3. Never turn your back on a bull.
  4. Use proper facilities: bull pens, crushes, races and strong gates.
  5. Lead bulls only with a nose ring and a bull pole, if you are trained.
  6. Watch for warning signs: pawing, head lowered, side-on display, snorting.
  7. Dairy bulls, especially Jersey and Holstein bulls, are known for being dangerous. Experience does not make them safe.

Moving cattle

  • Use low-stress handling: work at the edge of the flight zone, move slowly, avoid shouting.
  • Move cows at walking pace, especially on tracks to and from camps; rushing causes lameness and injury.
  • Do not use dogs, sticks or electric prodders on cows in milk.
  • Remove distractions in races, such as hanging chains, shadows and loose objects.

Animal welfare

The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 makes it an offence to cause unnecessary suffering. Treat sick and injured animals promptly, never leave a downer cow unattended, and make sure only animals fit to travel are loaded for sale.

Recording

Complete herd records the same day: heats, services, pregnancy results, treatments, dry-offs, lameness scores, movements and deaths.

Key points

  • Observe the herd at set times and record heats and problems.
  • Prepare cows calmly for AI and vet checks.
  • Give treatments only as instructed, at the correct site, and record withdrawal dates.
  • Never work alone with a bull and always have an escape route.
  • Move cattle slowly and humanely.

quiz.question: Rubbed-off tail paint on a cow suggests that:

options.text: She has been mounted and may be on heat

quiz.question: Why should injections be given in the neck rather than the rump?

options.text: It is easier to reach in the parlour

quiz.question: What must you check before using a tick treatment on a lactating cow?

options.text: The milk withdrawal time on the label

After cleaning each teat end with a separate swab
